name: Budapest Gallery
description: The Budapest Gallery is the contemporary-art arm of the Budapest History Museum. Its exhibition house at Lajos utca 158 in Óbuda occupies an old dwelling house whose recorded history goes back to the early eighteenth century, and it presents Hungarian and international art across painting, photography, design and architecture.

children.text: The Budapest Gallery shows contemporary Hungarian and international art, and its exhibition house stands at Lajos utca 158 in Óbuda. The gallery aims to present contemporary art to the public and to introduce Hungarian artists to audiences abroad, and its programme reaches beyond painting to architecture, photography, media art, applied arts and design.

The institution has had several names and homes. It was founded in 1979 as the Budapest Fine Arts Directorate, with one department for public art and one for fine art, and was renamed Budapest Gallery in 1983. In 2011 the city assembly made it a main department of the Budapest History Museum. Its exhibition department first worked from the Klotild Palace building in Szabadsajtó utca and moved in 2013 to the Bálna building on the Danube, where it ran the New Budapest Gallery until 2019.

The Lajos utca house itself has a long and modest history. A museum page records the building as a Bear House at the beginning of the eighteenth century, says it was rebuilt as a dwelling house toward the end of that century, and notes that further extensions were added in the nineteenth century. It is now the gallery's exhibition house.

Besides changing exhibitions of living artists, the house holds a permanent display of works by the sculptor Pál Pátzay, who lived from 1896 to 1976. The small statues in that exhibition, which opened in 1982, come from the Budapest History Museum's own collection. The gallery also looks after the Imre Varga Collection, devoted to another sculptor, which has its own address on Laktanya utca in the same district.
Good to know
The gallery is in Óbuda at Lajos utca 158; check the official site for the current exhibition programme, opening times and tickets.
Exhibitions change often, so look at the gallery's programme before you travel and see what is on.
The Imre Varga Collection on Laktanya utca is a separate site run by the same gallery, so confirm which venue a given exhibition uses.

historyIntro: Budapest Gallery connects the city's historic cultural spaces with new visual ideas and contemporary artistic debate.

historySections.heading: Exhibiting art within the city's history

children.text: The Gallery forms part of Budapest's city-museum network and has presented work by Hungarian and international contemporary artists. Rather than offering one fixed narrative, its temporary programmes track the changing questions explored by artists.

The museum's Óbuda location ties the modern exhibitions to a district with a long Roman, town and industrial heritage. That setting can be part of the experience even when the art on the walls is explicitly contemporary.

name: Hungarian Railway History Park
description: A railway museum in a former locomotive depot in Budapest's 14th district, with a 34-stall roundhouse, a turntable and more than a hundred vehicles from steam locomotives to rare railcars. Visitors can also try a locomotive simulator and see a small railway running through the grounds.

children.text: The Hungarian Railway History Park, Magyar Vasúttörténeti Park, stands at Tatai út 95 in Budapest's 14th district, on the site of the former Northern depot of the Hungarian State Railways. It covers more than 70,000 square metres and displays over a hundred vehicles and pieces of equipment, mostly railway vehicles.

The site has its own history. The depot was built in 1911 as a twin: a 22-stall building and a 34-stall building. Only the larger one survives, because the smaller was destroyed during the Second World War. The surviving roundhouse and turntable now display locomotives, which is why the park is full of engines standing in their old stalls. From 1951 to 1990 the depot carried the name Hámán Kató Fűtőház.

The museum's roots go back further than the park. A small railway open-air museum had operated at Ópaks station in Paks from 1985 to 2000, and the Hungarian Railway Museum Foundation was founded on 22 November 1999. The park itself opened on 14 July 2000.

The fleet runs from steam to electric traction, and some of it still works and is used for nostalgic trips in Hungary and abroad. Named exhibits include a teak dining car built for the Orient Express in 1912, the Árpád railcar of 1934, the steam locomotive MÁV 411.118 of the USATC S160 class and a Soviet GAZ-13 Chaika that served Prime Minister Jenő Fock and was later converted to run on rails.
Visitors can also ride the garden railway in the grounds, which the park's ticket information lists; check the park for its other hands-on attractions.
Good to know
Nearby bus stops are served by routes 30 and 30A, among others; Angyalföld station is about a 15-minute walk away. Check current routes before you set off.
A halt called Vasútmúzeum on the Budapest to Esztergom line is reported to be served only at weekends and on holidays, so confirm train times if you plan to arrive by rail.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and the dates of special events and train rides.

historyIntro: The Railway History Park preserves the machines and practices that helped connect Hungarian cities, industries and travellers in the age of steam.

children.text: Rail transport transformed the movement of people and goods through Hungary during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Engines, carriages and railway infrastructure reflect the engineering ambition that made those connections possible.

historySections.heading: A museum built for large machines

children.text: The Budapest park gathers historic railway equipment in an open-air setting. The vehicles reveal how technology, passenger comfort and industrial design changed, while operational demonstrations and visitor activities depend on the current programme.

name: Medieval Jewish Prayer House
description: A small vaulted prayer hall on the ground floor of a house in the Castle District's old Jewish quarter, with Hebrew wall paintings from the Ottoman period and tombstones in a side room off the gateway. Sources differ on how old the hall is, and it is again used for worship.

children.text: The Medieval Jewish Prayer House is at Táncsics Mihály utca 26 on the Buda Castle hill, in what was once the Jewish quarter of Buda. The Castle District heritage site describes the building as a single-storey, unpretentious burgher's house that preserves the remains of a medieval Jewish worship hall. It is run by the Budapest History Museum, whose exhibition there is called The Jewish population of Buda in the Middle Ages.

Visitors pass through a barrel-vaulted gateway. In a room to the left stand tombstones from the medieval and Ottoman periods; turning right leads to the worship hall, whose roof is supported by pillars. On the vault is a painting from the Ottoman era showing a drawn bow with a line from Hannah's prayer, The bows of warriors are shattered, and nearby fields with Stars of David carry a priestly blessing from the Book of Numbers.

Sources disagree on the building's dating. Museum and tourism pages say the prayer house was built at the end of the fourteenth century and uncovered in 1964 during monument-protection research, which also revealed seventeenth-century Jewish inscriptions. A 2018 article instead links the hall to the Ottoman period and says it was found in 1968 during postwar reconstruction, starting from two fresco fragments in the gateway. The scholar Sándor Scheiber decoded the lettering and attributed it to Jews of the Sephardic rite rather than the Ashkenazi rite first suspected.

The hall is not the only synagogue site on the street. A far larger Great Synagogue is recorded at number 23, built in 1461 and destroyed in the siege of 1686. Its ruins were found in 1964 by the archaeologist László Zolnay, who reburied them under a concrete slab, and they still lie beneath the courtyard of a Baroque palace.

After years as an exhibition space, the hall was renovated at the initiative of the Unified Hungarian Jewish Congregation and regained its religious function in the autumn of 2018. It holds about seventy people, was designed inside by Tibor Somlai and still serves as an exhibition space on weekdays.
Good to know
The house is at Táncsics Mihály utca 26 in the Castle District, a short walk from the other Buda Castle sights.
Because the hall is again used for worship, check the official site for current visiting arrangements, opening times and tickets before you go.
It is a small room, so a visit is short; combine it with the Castle Museum, which belongs to the same museum group.

historyIntro: The Medieval Jewish Prayer House offers a rare glimpse of Jewish community life inside Buda's historic Castle District.

children.text: The surviving building is linked to Jewish religious life in the medieval and Ottoman periods. Architectural details and painted inscriptions help reveal a community whose history is not always visible in the district's grander royal buildings.

historySections.heading: A small site with lasting significance

children.text: The Budapest History Museum's interpretation includes historic symbols, writing and related finds. As with other sites of religious heritage, its history should be approached with respect for the people and traditions represented.

name: Petőfi Museum of Literature
description: Hungary's national literary museum fills the Károlyi Palace, a classicist building where a prime minister was arrested in 1849 and the Hungarian National Council was formed in 1918. Its collections include the manuscript of Petőfi's National Song and a complete Vizsoly Bible, and it reopened in 2023.

children.text: The Petőfi Museum of Literature, Petőfi Irodalmi Múzeum, is housed in the Károlyi Palace at Károlyi utca 16, on the corner of Károlyi Mihály utca and Ferenczy István utca. It was founded in 1954 and took over the legacy of the Petőfi–Jókai House, which dated from 1909. Its first two years of exhibitions were held at the Hungarian National Museum, it received a palace at József nádor tér in 1955, and it moved into the Károlyi Palace in the spring of 1957.

The palace is described as one of Budapest's most important classicist monuments. It was rebuilt from 1832 to designs by the Viennese architect Anton Pius Riegl, with József Hofrichter leading the construction, and the new palace was inaugurated in 1841. In the Reform Era it housed the literary salon of László Bártfay, where Franz Liszt played. In January 1849 Lajos Batthyány, prime minister of the first responsible Hungarian government, was arrested there, and in October 1918 the Hungarian National Council was formed in the building.

Count Mihály Károlyi was its last private owner. After he emigrated in 1919 the state confiscated the palace (a heritage register dates this to 1920), and the capital took over the building in the late 1920s, in 1928 or 1929 depending on the source. The capital's picture gallery was based there until 1953, and the Petőfi Museum moved in four years later. Hungarian Wikipedia records auctions of the family's art in 1932 and of a library in 1937. Renovations took place in 1996 to 2000 and again in 2022, and the building reopened in January 2023 with a new permanent Petőfi exhibition.

The collections centre on Hungarian literature. They include the manuscript of Petőfi's National Song, the manuscript of József Attila's poem At the Danube, and a complete copy of the Vizsoly Bible, known as the Károlyi Bible. The museum also holds the literary estates of writers such as Mór Jókai, Zsigmond Móricz, Ferenc Karinthy, Tibor Déry and Antal Szerb, and exhibits a printing press of the Landerer and Heckenast firm.
Good to know
The palace is at Károlyi utca 16 in central Pest, near the inner-city walking routes; check the official site for opening times and tickets.
Check the official English pages for what is available to non-Hungarian readers, as well as the current exhibitions.

historyIntro: The Petőfi Museum of Literature brings literary manuscripts and national memory into the historic rooms of Károlyi Palace.

historySections.heading: A palace for the written word

children.text: The museum is housed in one of Budapest's notable classicist buildings. It collects and interprets writings and objects associated with Hungarian authors, allowing manuscripts and personal possessions to become historical evidence.

Sándor Petőfi remains strongly associated with the Hungarian national awakening and 1848 Revolution. A museum named after him also explores a wider range of literary voices, revealing how the country's changing identity has been expressed through literature.
